latin.176:
ANNOTATIO II.
De Sociorum Confessionis Augustanae Consensu Fundamentali & Dissensu Praeter-fundamentali, hujusque Ortu, Progressu & Exitu,
Ad Pag. Autoris 332. & 333.
§. I.
Consensus Fundamentalis Sociorum Confessionis Augustanae, respicit Fundamentum Christianae Religionis, seu Doctrinae Christianae, tam Theoreticae, quàm Practicae, quippe quarum Doctrinarum aliae Fundamentales, aliae Fundamentatae sunt. PRIORES, seu Fundamentales, accipiuntur VEL SENSU SCRIPTURARIO, & sunt Doctrinae de Christo, unico Salvatore nostro, Deo & Homine, reliquis Fundamentum praebiturae omnium summum, seu primum, 1. Cor. 3. v. 11. Aliud equidem Fundamentum nemo potest ponere &c. Nam per Christum hoc in loco, non solam Personam Christi, sed potissimum Doctrinam de Christo intelligendam esse, patet, tum ex Antecedentibus, tum ex Consequentibus. Ex Antecedentibus quidem: Quandoquidem Fundamentum (Christus) à Paulo, ceu prudenti Architecto, positum dicitur; Erat autem à Paulo non Christus ipse positus, sed Doctrina seu Evangelium de Christo, ceu Fundamentum omnium Doctrinarum Christianae Religionis, Doctrinae de Christo superaedificandarum. Ex Consequentibus, quia alii aliique, dicuntur Fundamento superaedificaturi, Aurum, Argentum, Lignum, Stipulas, i. e. Fundamentali de Christo Doctrinae, Fundamentatas plurimas, alias preciosiores ac utiles, alias minus preciosas ac futiles. Quin idem probatur ex Eph. 2. ubi unô eôdemque vigesimo versiculo, tàm Apostoli & Prophetae, i. e. Doctrinae Apostolorum & Prophetarum praecipuae, non autem Personae eorum, Fundamentum salutantur, quam Christus Lapis Angularis, i. e. Doctrina de Christo Principalissima & maximè Fundamentalis dicitur.
latin.177: VEL SENSU THEOLOGICO, & sunt Doctrinae, tam ad Religionem vel Fidem Christianam constituendam, quàm ad Fidei Christianae Finem, Animarum nostrarum Salutem consequendam, omninò necessariae, indeque communiter dicendae, modò Fundamentales Fidei, respectu ad Objectum, Fundamentato intrinsecum & essentiale; modò Fundamentales Salutis, respectu ad Finem, Fundamentato partim intrinsecum & essentialem, partim extrinsecum & extraessentialem, habito. Necessitatem autem istarum omnem determinante, in Scriptura S., Deô solô, idque vel explicitè, vel implicitè, per obviam cuivis consequentiam; itemque exclusivo non minus Sensu, quàm positivo, ut & dicat Deus, quaenam Necessariae Doctrinae sint; & non dictas ab eo Necessarias, sive explicitè, sive implicitè, eô ipsô à Necessitate Fidei & Salutis, non tamen pariter à varii Gradûs Utilitate, exemptas velit. Neque enim vel probabile est, vel ullo modo admittendum, ut Deus, universae Scripturae S. unicus quidem Autor habitus, in qua & Necessaria ad Fidem Salutemque, & minus necessaria promiscuè traduntur, necessaria etiam nonnulla subindè apertè significantur, vel non omnia necessaria ullo modo definivisse, sicque necessaria à minus necessariis non satis distinxisse, vel definitionem distinctionemque hanc humano arbitrio permisissse credendus sit; praesertim cùm cuncta, ad salutem necessaria, promiscuè, eóque ut talia, tradiderit. Vide haec fusius edocta Inquisit. in Arminian. Annot. XVII.
latin.178:
§. II.
Hinc illi demùm Fundamentaliter in Religione Fideque Christiana consentire Sensu Theologicô dicuntur, qui in omnibus à Deo ad Fidem & Salutem dictis necessariis consentiunt; Necessaria autem nec alia, nec plura, nec pauciora arbitrantur, quàm quae DEus talia in verbo suo jussit esse. E contrario, isti Fundamentaliter dissentiunt, qui vel in Necessariis Fidei & Salutis, à DEO sic dictis, discrepant, negando vel omnia, vel quaedam eorum, idque, vel quà Veritatem, vel quà Necessitatem; vel praeter Necessaria Divina, alia, citra verbum DEi, ceu talia, cudunt obtruduntque. Horum Dissensuum prior Juris magis est; posterior magis Facti. Priori modô Fundamentaliter dissentiunt à Protestantibus Sociniani; Posteriori ab iisdem Pontificii: Protestantes verò, seu Evangelici, Fundamentaliter inter se convenire intelliguntur utrôque modô, excipiendis tamen Protestantibus iis, qui Dogmata quaedam, sibi domestica, neque in Scriptura Sacra, vel quoad Veritatem, nedum Necessitatem, fundata, Necessaria nihilominus urgent, & talia abnuentes à se separant damnantque, eô ipsô, Fundamento, si non Fidei, strictè sic dictae, seu Theoriae Christianae, Charitatis tamen, seu Praxeos (quae Religioni Christianae, adeoque Fidei Christianae latius dictae, pars altera est) excidentes.
latin.179:
§. III.
Ita Protestantes inter se Fundamentaliter convenire à priori ostensum est; Constare idem à posteriori potest inductione Capitum Doctrinae Christianae Necessariorum Generalium: Enimverò conveniunt inter se (1.) Principio cognoscendi Christiana Dogmata omnia, saltèm necessaria cuncta, primo & unicô adaequato, nempe Scripturâ S. ideò unanimibus votis, tam sufficienti atque perfectâ, quàm satis perspicua Regulâ & normâ credendorum pariter ac agendorum Christianorum omnium necessariorum, Protestantibus habita; Secus ac Christianis reliquis quibuscunque, vel Synonymicè, vel aequivocè sic dictis, à Protestantibus in eo dissidentibus, quod vel principio Scripturae aliud coordinant, Scilicet Traditiones seu Verbum non-Scriptum, vel hoc alteri subordinant, puta vel Lumini Nativo, i. e. Rationi, vel Lumini Fictitio, i. e. Enthusiasmo; Dum è contrario Protestantes tàm Enthusiasmum, quàm Verbum non-Scriptum, Scripturae adversa, explodunt penitus; Rationem verò, utcunque illuminatam, non Principium probandi, sed nudum apprehendendi instrumentum arbitrantur. (2.) Elementorum Christianae Religionis in omnibus particulis suis ingenua infucatâque receptione ac professione, Symboli Scilicet Apostolici, Decalogi, Precationis Dominicae, & duorum duntaxat Sacramentorum, Signata sua non significantium tantùm, sed & exhibentium & obsignantium.
latin.180: [3.] Augustanae Confessioni, eidemque Invariatae, facta sincera adstipulatione, etiam quod ad X. ejusdem Articulum attinet, Germanicè hic, vel Latinè legatur, dummodò Species panis & vini, in Germanica editione memoratae, non sensu Pontificio, pro accidentibus eorum, sed sensu Lutherano, pro Symbolis Corporis & Sanguinis Christi, accipiantur. Unde Reformati Collocutores Lipsienses testati sunt, se nunquam non ad subsignandum Invariatae Confessioni paratos fore, totôque illi pectore adhaesuros, uti jam tum diximus Annotat. I., infrà verba ipsorum adducturi. Denique (4.) ipsius Formulae Concordiae strictè sic dictae, i. e. tùm Epitomes Articulorum quorundam controversorum, tùm solidae Declarationis ac Repetitionis eorundem, tàm quoad Substantiam, quam quoad Modos, admissione, exceptis duntaxat Modis duobus, alterô ad Articulum de Coena S., ad articulum de Persona Christi alterô pertinente, quorum tamen Modorum binorum diversitatem Fundamentum Fidei Christianae ne è longinquo quidem attingere, locis suis demonstrabimus. Vide interim Tractatulum nostrum German. de Consensu Protestantium fundamentali à §. 10. ad 24.
latin.181:
§. IV.
Itaque omnis Dissensus Protestantium, inter se, Praeter-Fundamentalis meritò audit, cujus & Ortus & Progressus & ἀκμὴ seu Fastigium, hoc loco per compendium recensenda. Initium dicti dissensûs ponendum in Controversia de Interpretatione verborum Coenae, quam aliam aliamque primi Reformatores tres, Carolostadius, Lutherus, & Zwinglius, Pontificiis abusibus opponendam, meditati fuerant non per omnia aequè commodam. Calixt. Jud. Controv. §. 47. Et Lutherus quidem, à Praeceptore quondam suo Petro de Aliaco, Cardinali Cammeracensi, haustam, & Pontificiis paucioribus melioribusque adhuc receptam, retinebat, quâ ita Corpus Christi de pane praedicari innuebat, ut cum pane manente Corpus Christi in usu Coenae conjungeretur. Tom. II. Wittenb. Lat. fol. 70. B. eóq; praedicaretur de pane ceu in pane contentum, per propositionem inusitatam quidem, interim propriam, ac Tropô Rhetoricô quocunque cassam. Carolostadius Pontificiis adversaturus magis, Propositionem Identicam comminiscebatur, Corpus Christi, (haud secus ac Pontificia communior Sententia,) Panem Coena Domini exturbaturus, quasi Christus acceptum, benedictum fractumque panem eumque solum discipulis suis dedisset, inter dandum verò, digito in corpus suum directo, de hoc, non autem de Pane, dixisset: Hoc est corpus meum. Zwinglius denique, medius inter duos, & Panem, & Corpus Christi in Coena, sed istum Corporali, hoc Spirituali modo retenturus, Corpus Christi de Pane impropriè praedicari docebat improprietate omnibus Propositionibus Sacramentalibus communi, quâ per Metonymiam, Signatum de Signo dicitur, quod per signum significatur, modoque spirituali exhibetur.
latin.182: Media seu Carolostadii interpretatio, ceu Fabulosa & Historiolam quandam, extra Scripturam confictam, haud absimilem Fabulae socinianae, verbis Joh. 1. v. 3. Et verbum erat apud Deum, assuta (quâ Deitati Christi infesti imminent Sociniani) in medium adducens, adstipulatores invenit paucissimos, & paulò post evanuit, residuis duabus, alterâ in superiori Germania, in Inferiori alterâ, tantò majori cum animi contentione edoctis, quantò sibi initiò videbantur invicem obnitentes magis. Illa Corporalem Localemve in pane Corporis Christi praesentiam; Haec verò nullam omnino, & ne Spiritualem quidem praesentiam admittere primô intuitu visa. Illa in subsidium corporis Christi Ubiquitatem, praeteritis inauditam Seculis; Haec ejusdem Corporis ad dextram Dei in coelis Sessionem, in qua ascenderat, assumens.

pass_a.176: ANNOTATION II. On the Fundamental Consensus of the Associates of the Augsburg Confession and their Praeter-fundamental Dissensus, and of this latter's Origin, Progress, and Exit. To the Author's Page 332 and 333. §. I. The Fundamental Consensus of the Associates of the Augsburg Confession regards the Foundation of the Christian Religion, or of Christian Doctrine, both Theoretical and Practical, inasmuch as of those Doctrines some are Fundamental, others Fundamentata. The FORMER, or Fundamental ones, are taken EITHER IN THE SCRIPTURAL SENSE, and are the Doctrines concerning Christ, our only Saviour, God and Man, which are to afford to the rest the highest, or first, Foundation of all, 1 Cor. 3:11. For other foundation can no man lay, &c. For by Christ in this place, not only the Person of Christ, but chiefly the Doctrine concerning Christ is to be understood, is plain both from the Antecedents and from the Consequents. From the Antecedents indeed: Since the Foundation (Christ) is said to have been laid by Paul, as by a prudent Architect; but it was not Christ himself that was laid by Paul, but the Doctrine or Gospel concerning Christ, as the Foundation of all the Doctrines of the Christian Religion that are to be built upon the Doctrine concerning Christ. From the Consequents, because others and still others are said to be about to build upon the Foundation gold, silver, wood, stubble, i.e. upon the Fundamental Doctrine concerning Christ many Fundamentata, some more precious and useful, others less precious and futile. Nay, the same is proved from Eph. 2, where in one and the same twentieth verse both Apostles and Prophets, i.e. the chief Doctrines of the Apostles and Prophets, not however their Persons, are saluted as Foundation, and Christ as Corner-stone, i.e. the Doctrine concerning Christ is called the most Principal and most Fundamental.
pass_a.177: OR IN THE THEOLOGICAL SENSE, and they are Doctrines altogether necessary both for constituting the Christian Religion or Faith and for attaining the End of the Christian Faith, the Salvation of our Souls, and thence commonly to be called, now Fundamentals of Faith, with respect to the Object, the intrinsic and essential Fundamentatum; now Fundamentals of Salvation, with respect to the End, the Fundamentatum partly intrinsic and essential, partly extrinsic and extra-essential being had. But with God alone in Holy Scripture determining all the necessity of these, and that either explicitly or implicitly, by a consequence obvious to anyone; and likewise in an exclusive Sense no less than a positive, so that God both may say which Doctrines are Necessary, and may will those not said by him to be Necessary, whether explicitly or implicitly, by that very fact exempted from the Necessity of Faith and Salvation, yet not equally from Utility of various Degree. For it is neither probable, nor in any way to be admitted, that God, held indeed as the sole Author of the whole of Holy Scripture, in which both things Necessary to Faith and Salvation and less necessary things are handed down promiscuously, and some necessary things are also now and then openly signified, should be believed either not to have defined all necessary things in any way, and so not to have sufficiently distinguished the necessary from the less necessary, or to have left this definition and distinction to human arbitrium; especially since he has handed down promiscuously all things necessary to salvation, and therefore as such. See these things more fully taught in the Inquisition into the Arminians, Annotation XVII.
pass_a.178: §. II. Hence those at last are said to consent Fundamentally in the Christian Religion and Faith in the Theological Sense who consent in all things said by God as necessary to Faith and Salvation; and they judge the Necessary to be neither other, nor more, nor fewer, than those which God has commanded to be such in his word. On the contrary, those dissent Fundamentally who either disagree in the Necessaries of Faith and Salvation so said by GOD, by denying either all or some of them, and that either as to Truth or as to Necessity; or who beyond the Divine Necessaries forge and thrust forward other things, apart from the word of God, as such. Of these Dissents the former is more of Right; the latter more of Fact. In the former mode the Socinians dissent Fundamentally from the Protestants; in the latter the Pontificians from the same: but the Protestants, or Evangelicals, are understood to agree Fundamentally among themselves in both modes, those Protestants however being excepted who nevertheless urge as Necessary certain Dogmas domestic to themselves, founded neither in Sacred Scripture as to Truth, much less as to Necessity, and who separate and condemn from themselves those refusing such things, by that very fact falling away from the Foundation, if not of Faith strictly so called, or of Christian Theory, yet of Charity, or of Practice (which is the other part of the Christian Religion, and so of the Christian Faith more broadly so called).
pass_a.179: §. III. Thus that the Protestants agree Fundamentally among themselves has been shown a priori; the same can be made to stand a posteriori by induction of the General Necessary Heads of Christian Doctrine: For they agree among themselves (1.) in the Principle of knowing all Christian Dogmas, at least all the necessary ones, the first and sole adequate principle, namely Holy Scripture, and therefore held by Protestants with unanimous votes as a Rule and norm both sufficient and perfect and sufficiently clear of all necessary things to be believed equally and to be done by Christians; Unlike the remaining Christians of whatever sort, whether synonymously or equivocally so called, who differ from the Protestants in this, that they either coordinate something else with the principle of Scripture, namely Traditions or the Unwritten Word, or subordinate this to something else, for example either to Native Light, i.e. Reason, or to Fictitious Light, i.e. Enthusiasm; While on the contrary the Protestants thoroughly explode both Enthusiasm and the Unwritten Word as adverse to Scripture; but they judge Reason, however illuminated, not a Principle of proving, but a bare instrument of apprehending. (2.) in the ingenuous and unpainted reception and profession of the Elements of the Christian Religion in all their particles, namely of the Apostles' Symbol, of the Decalogue, of the Lord's Prayer, and of only two Sacraments, which not only signify their Signified things but also exhibit and seal them.
pass_a.180: [3.] in sincere adhesion made to the Augsburg Confession, and to the same as Invariata, even as regards its Tenth Article, whether it be read here in German or in Latin, provided that the Species of bread and wine mentioned in the German edition be taken not in the Pontifical sense, for their accidents, but in the Lutheran sense, for Symbols of the Body and Blood of Christ. Whence the Reformed Colloquists of Leipzig have testified that they would never not be ready to subscribe the Invariata Confession, and would adhere to it with their whole breast, as we already then said in Annotation I., being about to bring in their words below. Finally (4.) in the admission of the Formula of Concord strictly so called, i.e. both of the Epitome of certain controversial Articles and of the solid Declaration and Repetition of the same, both as to Substance and as to Modes, excepting only two Modes, the one pertaining to the Article on the Holy Supper, the other to the article on the Person of Christ, whose diversity of these two Modes, however, we shall demonstrate in their places does not even from afar touch the Foundation of the Christian Faith. See meanwhile our German Tractate on the fundamental Consensus of the Protestants from §. 10 to 24.
pass_a.181: §. IV. Therefore every Dissensus of the Protestants among themselves is deservedly called Praeter-Fundamental, whose Origin and Progress and peak (akme) or Summit are to be reviewed in this place by a compendium. The beginning of the said dissensus is to be placed in the Controversy concerning the Interpretation of the words of the Supper, which the three first Reformers, Carlstadt, Luther, and Zwingli, had contemplated, each differently, as to be opposed to Pontifical abuses, not equally convenient in all respects. Calixtus, Judgment of Controversies §. 47. And Luther indeed retained that drawn from his sometime Preceptor Peter d'Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, and still received by the fewer and better Pontificians, by which he implied that the Body of Christ is predicated of the bread in such a way that, the bread remaining, the Body of Christ is joined with the bread in the use of the Supper. Tom. II Wittenberg Latin fol. 70 B; and thus it would be predicated of the bread as contained in the bread, by a proposition unusual indeed, yet proper meanwhile, and void of any Rhetorical Trope whatever. Carlstadt, about to oppose the Pontificians more, invented an Identical Proposition, about to drive out the Bread of the Lord's Supper by the Body of Christ (just as the more common Pontifical Opinion), as if Christ had given to his disciples the bread received, blessed, and broken, and that alone, but while giving, with his finger directed to his own body, had said of this, not of the Bread: This is my body. Zwingli finally, middle between the two, about to retain both Bread and the Body of Christ in the Supper, but the former in a Corporeal, the latter in a Spiritual mode, taught that the Body of Christ is improperly predicated of the Bread by an impropriety common to all Sacramental Propositions, by which through Metonymy the Signified is said of the Sign, which is signified through the sign and is exhibited in a spiritual mode.
pass_a.182: The middle or Carlstadt's interpretation, as Fabulous and bringing into the midst a certain little History forged outside Scripture, not unlike the Socinian Fable stitched onto the words of John 1:3 'And the word was with God' (by which the Socinians hostile to Christ's Deity threaten), found very few adherents, and a little later vanished, the two remaining being taught with so much greater contention of mind, the one in upper Germany, the other in Lower, the more they at first seemed to themselves to be mutually resisting. That one a Corporeal or Local presence of Christ's Body in the bread; This one, however, at first glance seemed to admit no presence at all, and not even a Spiritual one. That one assuming in support the Ubiquity of Christ's body, unheard-of in past Ages; This one the Session of the same Body at the right hand of God in the heavens, into which it had ascended.

176: ANNOTATION II. On the Augsburg Confession associates' fundamental consensus and their praeter-fundamental dissent — and on that dissent's origin, progress, and outcome. To the Author's pp. 332–333.

§. I. The associates' fundamental consensus looks to the foundation of the Christian religion — Christian doctrine, theoretical and practical — of which some doctrines are fundamentals and others are built on them (fundamentata).

The former, taken in the scriptural sense, are the doctrines concerning Christ, our only Saviour, God and Man: the highest, first foundation for everything else ([[1 Cor. 3:11 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 3:11]]: "For other foundation can no man lay," &c.).

Here "Christ" means chiefly the doctrine about Christ, not only his person — clear from what precedes and what follows. Paul as wise architect is said to have laid the foundation (Christ); what he laid was not Christ himself but the gospel-doctrine about Christ, the base on which other Christian doctrines are built.

What follows confirms it: others are to build on that foundation gold, silver, wood, stubble — many things founded on the fundamental doctrine of Christ, some precious and useful, some cheaper and futile.

[[Eph. 2:20 >> Bible:Ephesians 2:20]] says the same in one verse: Apostles and Prophets (i.e. their chief doctrines, not their persons) are called foundation, and Christ the cornerstone — that is, the doctrine of Christ is named the principal and most fundamental.
177: Or take fundamentals in the theological sense: doctrines wholly necessary both to constitute Christian religion or faith and to reach faith's end — the salvation of our souls.

Hence they are commonly called either fundamentals of faith (toward the object: the intrinsic, essential thing founded) or fundamentals of salvation (toward the end: the thing founded partly intrinsic/essential, partly extrinsic/extra-essential).

God alone in Holy Scripture fixes all that necessity — explicitly or implicitly, by a consequence open to anyone — and in an exclusive sense no less than a positive one: so God both names which doctrines are necessary and, by not naming others as necessary (explicitly or implicitly), exempts them from faith-and-salvation necessity, though not from usefulness of every degree.

It is neither likely nor admissible that God, sole author of all Scripture — where necessities for faith and salvation are mixed with lesser matters, and some necessities are at times marked openly — either failed to define all necessities at all (and so failed to distinguish them from the less necessary) or left that definition and distinction to human whim; especially since he handed down everything needed for salvation promiscuously, and as such. See this taught more fully in the Inquisition into the Arminians, Annotation XVII.
178: §. II. Those finally are said to agree fundamentally in Christian religion and faith, in the theological sense, who agree in everything God has called necessary to faith and salvation — and who count as necessary neither other things, nor more, nor fewer, than God has commanded to be such in his word.

Those dissent fundamentally who either diverge from the necessaries of faith and salvation so named by God, denying all or some of them as to truth or as to necessity; or who, beyond the divine necessaries, forge and push other things as necessary apart from God's word.
Of these dissents the former is more a matter of right; the latter more of fact. Socinians dissent fundamentally from Protestants in the former way; Romanists in the latter.

Protestants, or Evangelicals, are understood to agree fundamentally among themselves in both ways — except those who still press as necessary certain house-dogmas of their own, founded neither in Scripture as to truth nor (still less) as to necessity, and who cut off and damn those who refuse them: thereby falling from the foundation, if not of faith strictly so called (Christian theory), then of charity or practice (the other part of the Christian religion, and of Christian faith in the wider sense).
179: §. III. That Protestants agree fundamentally among themselves has already been shown a priori; the same can be confirmed a posteriori by running through the general necessary heads of Christian doctrine.

(1.) They agree on the first and only adequate principle for knowing all Christian dogmas — at least all the necessary ones — namely Holy Scripture: held by Protestants with one voice as a rule and norm, both sufficient and perfect and clear enough, for everything Christians must believe and must do.

Other so-called Christians (synonymously or only equivocally) differ here: they either set something beside Scripture as co-principle — Traditions, the unwritten word — or put Scripture under something else, native light (reason) or fictitious light (enthusiasm).

Protestants, by contrast, explode enthusiasm and the unwritten word as hostile to Scripture; and they treat reason, however illuminated, not as a principle of proof but as a bare instrument of apprehension.

(2.) They agree in an honest, unvarnished reception and profession of the elements of Christian religion in all their parts: the Apostles' Creed, the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer, and only two sacraments — which not only signify their significates but also exhibit and seal them.
180: (3.) They agree in sincere adhesion to the Augsburg Confession — and to it as Invariata — even on Article X, whether the German or the Latin is read here, provided the "species" of bread and wine in the German edition are taken not in the Roman sense (as accidents) but in the Lutheran sense (as symbols of Christ's body and blood).

Hence the Reformed colloquists at Leipzig testified they would always be ready to subscribe the Invariata Confession and cling to it with their whole heart — as we already said in Annotation I, and will quote their words below.

(4.) They agree in admitting the Formula of Concord strictly so called — both the Epitome of certain disputed articles and the Solid Declaration and Repetition of the same — as to substance and as to modes, except only two modes: one on the Holy Supper, the other on the Person of Christ.

Even that twofold modal diversity, we shall show in due place, does not touch the foundation of the Christian faith even from afar. See meanwhile our German tract on the Protestants' fundamental consensus, §§. 10–24.
181: §. IV. So every dissent among Protestants is rightly called praeter-fundamental. Its origin, progress, and peak (akme) may be sketched here in brief.

That dissent begins in the controversy over interpreting the words of the Supper — which the three first Reformers, Carlstadt, Luther, and Zwingli, each framed differently as a counter to Roman abuses, and not equally handy in every respect (Calixtus, Judgment of Controversies §. 47).

Luther kept the line drawn from his former teacher Peter d'Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, and still held by the fewer and better Romanists: that Christ's body is predicated of the bread so that, the bread remaining, Christ's body is joined with the bread in the Supper's use (Wittenberg Latin Tom. II, fol. 70 B) — predicated of the bread as contained in the bread, by a proposition unusual yet proper, and empty of any rhetorical trope.

Carlstadt, pressing the Romans harder, invented an identical proposition: driving the bread of the Lord's Supper out by Christ's body (much as the more common Roman view), as if Christ had given his disciples only the received, blessed, broken bread, and while giving, pointing to his own body, had said of that — not of the bread — "This is my body."

Zwingli, midway between them, meant to keep both bread and Christ's body in the Supper — the bread corporally, the body spiritually — and taught that Christ's body is improperly predicated of the bread by the impropriety common to all sacramental propositions: by metonymy the significate is said of the sign, which signifies it and exhibits it spiritually.
182: Carlstadt's middle reading — fabulous, and dragging in a little story forged outside Scripture, not unlike the Socinian fable stitched onto [[John 1:3 >> Bible:John 1:3]] "And the word was with God" (by which Socinians hostile to Christ's deity press their case) — found very few backers and soon vanished.
The other two remained, taught with all the more heat — one in upper Germany, the other in Lower — the more they first seemed to clash.
The one: a corporeal or local presence of Christ's body in the bread. The other: at first glance seeming to admit no presence at all, not even a spiritual one.
The former called in aid the ubiquity of Christ's body, unheard of in past ages; the latter, that body's session at God's right hand in the heavens into which it had ascended.
